questions.question: What is the etymological origin and literal definition of the word 'philosophy'?
options: From Latin 'philo' (system) and 'sophia' (science), meaning systematic science
From Greek 'philo' (love) and 'sophia' (wisdom), meaning love of wisdom
From Greek 'philos' (truth) and 'anthropos' (man), meaning study of humanity
From Latin 'physis' (nature) and 'logos' (word), meaning discourse on nature
questions.explanation: Etymologically, philosophy comes from two Greek words: 'philo' (love) and 'sophia' (wisdom), meaning literally 'love of wisdom'[cite: 195].

questions.question: Who was the ancient Greek thinker that first used the term 'philosopher' to describe a person with marked curiosity about experience?
options: Aristotle
Pythagoras
Socrates
Plato
questions.explanation: Pythagoras was the first to use the word 'philosopher' to call a person showing curiosity in experiencing the world[cite: 195].

questions.question: According to Socrates, what is the fundamental origin of philosophy?
options: Philosophy begins in empirical measurement
Philosophy begins in wonder
Philosophy begins in social rebellion
Philosophy begins in religious revelation
questions.explanation: Socrates famously proclaimed that 'Wonder is the feeling of a philosopher, and philosophy begins in wonder'[cite: 194].

questions.question: How does the module distinguish the wisdom sought by philosophers from ordinary technical expertise?
options: It consists of accumulating vast amounts of commercial information
It is the development of critical habits, continuous search for truth, and questioning the apparent
It is the memorization of scientific formulas
It is identical to professional vocational training
questions.explanation: Philosophical wisdom is not technical expertise; it consists of a critical habit, eternal vigilance, reverence for truth, and questioning the apparent[cite: 195].

questions.question: What does it mean to 'question the apparent' in philosophical inquiry?
options: To completely deny the physical existence of reality
To go beyond common understanding and speculate creatively about things accepted without doubt
To reject all forms of logical thought
To accept social dogmas unconditionally
questions.explanation: Questioning the apparent means to deal creatively with the phenomenal world, moving beyond common sense to speculate rigorously[cite: 195, 196].

questions.question: What are the two interrelated dimensions that constitute the philosophical enterprise?
options: A mathematical side and a biological side
A constructive side and a critical side
A subjective side and an emotional side
A dogmatic side and a passive side
questions.explanation: Philosophy has a constructive side (formulating defensible answers) and a critical side (rational analysis and evaluation of answers)[cite: 196].

questions.question: How does the informal sense of philosophy ('having' a philosophy) differ from the formal sense ('doing' philosophy)?
options: 'Having' refers to personal uncritical beliefs; 'doing' refers to active critical reflection and examination
'Having' is restricted to academics; 'doing' is practiced by ordinary citizens
'Doing' means memorizing history; 'having' means writing a book
There is no difference between the two senses
questions.explanation: Having a philosophy refers to an informal set of unexamined beliefs, whereas doing philosophy is critical, systematic reflection[cite: 197].

questions.question: Why do philosophers frequently disagree with one another according to the text?
options: Because logic is entirely arbitrary
Due to different points of view/assumptions, changing societies, and incomplete evidence
Because philosophers refuse to use reason
Because language has no cognitive meaning
questions.explanation: Philosophers disagree because they view things from different assumptions/backgrounds, live in a dynamic universe, and deal with incomplete evidence[cite: 198].

questions.question: Which basic feature of philosophy emphasizes synthesizing scientific findings and human experiences into a unified worldview?
options: Logical analysis of language
Philosophy as a rational attempt to look at the world as a whole
Philosophy as an informal set of dogmas
Specialized experimental testing
questions.explanation: Philosophy attempts to view life as a totality, combining the conclusions of various sciences into a consistent worldview[cite: 198].

questions.question: What is the primary role of philosophy according to twentieth-century linguistic analysts?
options: Constructing grand metaphysical worldviews
Exposing confusion and nonsense through logical analysis of language and clarification of concepts
Developing speculative religious doctrines
Replacing all scientific inquiry
questions.explanation: Linguistic analysts view philosophy's main task as the logical analysis of language, exposing nonsense, and clarifying terms[cite: 199].

questions.question: What are the four primary branches of philosophy discussed in this course?
options: Physics, chemistry, biology, and geology
Metaphysics, epistemology, axiology, and logic
Psychology, sociology, anthropology, and ethics
Theology, cosmology, ontology, and aesthetics
questions.explanation: The primary core branches of philosophy are metaphysics, epistemology, axiology, and logic[cite: 201].

questions.question: How did the term 'metaphysics' originate historically?
options: It was coined by Socrates during his trial
Aristotle's editor, Andronicus of Rhodes, named Aristotle's works on 'first philosophy' that came after his physics treatise 'meta ta physika'
It was invented by medieval scholastic theologians
It was derived from Plato's allegory of the cave
questions.explanation: Andronicus of Rhodes coined 'metaphysics' ('after physics') for Aristotle's works on first philosophy placed after his treatise on physics[cite: 202].

questions.question: What is the central subject matter of metaphysics?
options: The study of valid arguments
The study of the ultimate nature of reality or existence
The study of sensory perceptions
The study of civic governance
questions.explanation: Metaphysics investigates the ultimate nature of reality, existence, mind-body relation, God, and first principles[cite: 202].

questions.question: Which subset of metaphysics focuses on theories concerning the origin, nature, and development of the universe as an orderly system?
options: Theology
Cosmology
Anthropology
Ontology
questions.explanation: Cosmology is the metaphysical study of theories about the origin, nature, and development of the universe[cite: 203].

questions.question: Which aspect of metaphysics examines questions regarding God's existence, attributes, and the problem of evil?
options: Ontological aspect
Theological aspect
Anthropological aspect
Cosmological aspect
questions.explanation: Theological metaphysics deals with conceptions of God, divine attributes, and relations to the created world[cite: 203].

questions.question: The metaphysical study of the nature of human existence, including free will vs. determinism and the mind-body problem, belongs to:
options: Cosmology
Anthropological aspect
Semiotics
Applied ethics
questions.explanation: Anthropological metaphysics investigates human nature, free will, the relation of mind and body, and the soul[cite: 203].

questions.question: Ontology is formally defined as the study of:
options: Artistic beauty and taste
The nature of existence, or what it means for anything to exist
Deductive syllogistic rules
Linguistic syntax and phonemes
questions.explanation: Ontology is the branch of metaphysics that studies the nature of existence and being as such[cite: 204].

questions.question: What is the primary concern of epistemology?
options: The moral codes of social institutions
The nature, source, scope, validity, and limits of human knowledge
The physical constituents of atomic matter
The grammatical classification of prepositions
questions.explanation: Epistemology ('theory of knowledge') investigates the nature, sources, scope, and dependability of knowledge[cite: 204].

questions.question: Which philosophical position claims that genuine, reliable knowledge is impossible to acquire and the search for truth is in vain?
options: Rationalism
Skepticism
Empiricism
Authoritarianism
questions.explanation: Skepticism is the philosophical stance asserting that humans cannot acquire reliable knowledge[cite: 205].

questions.question: How is agnosticism distinguished from pure skepticism in epistemology?
options: Agnosticism claims all knowledge is innate
Agnosticism is specifically a profession of ignorance regarding the existence or nonexistence of God
Agnosticism asserts that only mathematical knowledge is true
Agnosticism rejects all sensory experience
questions.explanation: Agnosticism is a profession of ignorance specifically concerning the existence or nonexistence of God[cite: 205].

questions.question: Empiricism identifies which faculty as the primary source of human knowledge?
options: Pure abstract deduction
Sense perception and sensory experience
Supernatural divine revelation
Mystical intuition
questions.explanation: Empiricism maintains that sensory experience (seeing, hearing, touching, etc.) is the basis of knowledge[cite: 205].

questions.question: What is a major limitation of relying exclusively on sensory perception for knowledge?
options: Sensory perceptions cannot be verified by other observers
Human senses can be deceived by optical illusions, fatigue, and physical limitations
Sensory data requires no mental interpretation
Senses provide only mathematical certainties
questions.explanation: Sensory data is often incomplete, distorted by physical/mental states (such as a bent stick in water), and limited in range[cite: 206].

questions.question: Rationalism asserts that the central factor in arriving at genuine knowledge is:
options: Random trial and error
Human reason, thought, and intellectual logic
Subconscious intuition alone
The blind acceptance of traditional dogmas
questions.explanation: Rationalism holds that reasoning and the mind's intellect are the essential factors in knowledge, independent of raw sensation[cite: 206].

questions.question: How is intuition defined as an epistemological source of knowledge?
options: The step-by-step application of categorical syllogisms
The direct, immediate apprehension of insight occurring beneath the threshold of conscious reasoning
The sensory inspection of external empirical objects
Consulting an encyclopedia or legal document
questions.explanation: Intuition is immediate insight or knowing that bypasses conscious sequential reasoning or sensory perception[cite: 207].

questions.question: What distinguishes revelation from all other sources of human knowledge?
options: It is discovered solely in physics laboratories
It presupposes a transcendent, supernatural reality breaking into the natural order to communicate divine truth
It is universally open to direct sensory replication
It requires no personal belief or faith
questions.explanation: Revealed knowledge presupposes a supernatural divine reality communicating truths not accessible via ordinary human faculties[cite: 207].

questions.question: What danger is associated with accepting authority as a primary source of knowledge?
options: It makes communication impossible
If authoritative claims rest on flawed assumptions or bias, the resulting knowledge will be distorted
Authoritative knowledge is always completely false
It forces people to rely entirely on intuition
questions.explanation: While necessary for civilization, authoritative knowledge is dangerous if built on incorrect assumptions or uncritical traditions[cite: 207, 208].

questions.question: Axiology is derived from the Greek words 'axios' and 'logos', which translate to:
options: Study of physical motion
Study or theory of value and worth
Theory of grammar and syntax
Science of planetary orbits
questions.explanation: Axiology stems from 'axios' (worth, value) and 'logos' (study/theory), meaning the philosophical study of value[cite: 209].

questions.question: What are the three principal areas of inquiry within axiology?
options: Mechanics, dynamics, and statics
Ethics, aesthetics, and social/political philosophy
Cosmology, theology, and ontology
Connotation, denotation, and semiotics
questions.explanation: Axiology deals with human values across three distinct fields: Ethics, Aesthetics, and Social/Political Philosophy[cite: 209].

questions.question: How is ethics (moral philosophy) formally defined?
options: The mechanical study of legal statutes
The philosophical study of moral principles, rules, and values used to judge conduct as right or wrong
The historical analysis of ancient tribal customs
The calculation of financial profitability
questions.explanation: Ethics is the philosophical inquiry into moral values and principles that determine right and wrong human actions[cite: 209, 210].

questions.question: What are the three major branches of ethical studies?
options: Linear ethics, circular ethics, and static ethics
Normative ethics, meta-ethics, and applied ethics
Subjective ethics, physical ethics, and psychological ethics
Formal ethics, syllogistic ethics, and modal ethics
questions.explanation: Ethics is categorized into normative ethics, meta-ethics, and applied ethics[cite: 210, 211].

questions.question: Which branch of ethics attempts to establish the moral standards, principles, and theories (e.g., deontology, utilitarianism) governing right action?
options: Meta-ethics
Normative ethics
Applied ethics
Aesthetic ethics
questions.explanation: Normative ethics searches for foundational principles and standards determining which acts are right or good[cite: 210].

questions.question: Meta-ethics is primarily concerned with:
options: Prescribing rules for business management
Investigating the meaning of ethical terms (e.g., 'good', 'right') and the epistemological status of moral claims
Resolving concrete dilemmas such as abortion and euthanasia
Codifying international environmental treaties
questions.explanation: Meta-ethics examines the meaning, nature, and justification of moral terminology and moral statements[cite: 210, 211].

questions.question: Applying general moral principles to specific controversial issues such as capital punishment, euthanasia, and abortion is the domain of:
options: Ontology
Applied ethics
Meta-ethics
Cosmology
questions.explanation: Applied ethics takes general ethical theories and applies them to specific real-world moral problems[cite: 211].

questions.question: Aesthetics is the branch of axiology that studies:
options: The distribution of economic wealth in civil society
The nature of beauty, art, taste, and sensory-emotional evaluations
The deductive validity of categorical syllogisms
The physical laws of gravitational motion
questions.explanation: Aesthetics is the philosophical study of art, beauty, aesthetic experiences, and standards of taste[cite: 211].

questions.question: Which of the following is a central question of social and political philosophy?
options: What is the atomic composition of carbon?
What makes a government legitimate and what is the nature of justice in society?
How do sound waves refract across water?
Is the external world an illusion of the senses?
questions.explanation: Social/political philosophy examines the justification of the state, justice, civil obligations, and ideal forms of society[cite: 212].

questions.question: How is logic defined as a core branch of philosophy?
options: The empirical measurement of neurological brainwaves
The philosophical study of arguments and the principles and methods of correct reasoning
The study of ancient political constitutions
The classification of moral codes across cultures
questions.explanation: Logic is the systematic study of arguments and the principles that distinguish good reasoning from bad reasoning[cite: 212, 221, 222].

questions.question: Socrates' famous dictum concerning the purpose of philosophical inquiry states that:
options: Might makes right
The unexamined life is not worth living
Truth is purely subjective opinion
Philosophy is an impossible science
questions.explanation: Socrates declared that 'the unexamined life is not worth living' to emphasize critical self-examination[cite: 213].

questions.question: How do psychologists categorize human needs, and how does philosophy assist with them?
options: Basic and biological; philosophy provides material food
Maintenance needs (food, shelter) and actualizing needs (self-fulfillment, creativity); philosophy promotes self-actualization
Sensory and mechanical; philosophy eliminates all physical needs
Conscious and subconscious; philosophy is an unconscious process
questions.explanation: Humans have maintenance needs (physical survival) and actualizing needs (creativity, fulfillment); philosophy contributes to self-actualization[cite: 213, 214].

questions.question: Which benefit of studying philosophy refers to the ability to develop one's own coherent, systematic worldview independently?
options: Authoritative obedience
Intellectual and behavioral independence
Dogmatic skepticism
Emotional indulgence
questions.explanation: Philosophy fosters intellectual and behavioral independence by helping individuals construct their own reasoned worldviews[cite: 214].

questions.question: According to Bertrand Russell, where is the ultimate value of philosophy largely to be found?
options: In proving absolute religious doctrines with scientific instruments
In its very uncertainty, which frees our minds from the tyranny of custom and dogmatism
In providing marketable technical skills for commercial industries
In producing dogmatic answers to everyday factual disputes
questions.explanation: Bertrand Russell argued that philosophy's value lies in its uncertainty, liberating us from narrow prejudices and keeping alive our sense of wonder[cite: 215].

questions.question: The philosophical approach that views reality as fundamentally spiritual or mental rather than purely physical is known as:
options: Materialism
Idealism
Behaviorism
Pragmatism
questions.explanation: Idealism is the philosophical theory maintaining that fundamental reality is mental, spiritual, or idea-based[cite: 200, 204].

questions.question: George Knight's illustration of a floor (viewed differently by an ordinary person, a physicist, and a chemist) demonstrates that:
options: Floors do not exist at all
The question of reality is multi-layered and foundational to metaphysical inquiry
Chemistry is superior to philosophy
Common sense always provides the final truth
questions.explanation: The floor example shows that reality presents profound levels of description, proving that metaphysical reality is not simplistic[cite: 202, 203].

questions.question: Which meta-ethical view claims that moral judgments merely express personal emotional feelings or attitudes rather than cognitive facts?
options: Moral Intuitionism
Moral Emotivism
Moral Realism
Deontology
questions.explanation: Emotivism holds that moral statements do not state facts but merely express emotional attitudes of approval or disapproval[cite: 210, 211].

questions.question: What is the primary role of logic in relation to other philosophical investigations?
options: Logic provides historical dates of philosophical texts
Logic serves as both a field of study and an indispensable tool to formulate and critically evaluate arguments
Logic is solely concerned with empirical biology
Logic replaces the need for epistemological inquiry
questions.explanation: Logic is both an academic field and an instrument used by philosophers to evaluate arguments and clarify reasoning[cite: 193, 221, 222].

questions.question: If an epistemologist argues that human knowledge is limited to statements about observable facts and their physical interrelations, they adopt:
options: A narrow positivist or empiricist perspective
A metaphysical theological theory
An intuitionist framework
A radical skepticism
questions.explanation: Restricting genuine knowledge to empirically verifiable facts reflects the narrow view of logical positivism and radical empiricism[cite: 199, 274].

questions.question: What is a 'worldview' in the context of philosophy?
options: An atlas containing physical boundary maps
A comprehensive, unified, and consistent interpretation of life, the universe, and human experience
A specialized handbook on industrial engineering
A transient emotional mood
questions.explanation: A worldview is a coherent, comprehensive perspective on the whole of reality that synthesizes diverse areas of human inquiry[cite: 198, 214].

questions.question: Why is philosophy considered an 'activity' rather than a static body of memorized doctrines?
options: Because philosophers must run physical races
Because genuine philosophy consists of the ongoing dynamic exercise of questioning, analyzing, and philosophizing
Because philosophy cannot be written in textbooks
Because philosophical theories change every hour
questions.explanation: Philosophy is fundamentally an activity: mastering philosophy means engaging actively in critical analysis, questioning, and evaluation[cite: 196].

questions.question: The philosophical discipline that examines ethical obligations, rights, and responsibilities regarding animal treatment and environmental protection is:
options: Meta-ethics
Applied ethics
Ontology
Epistemology
questions.explanation: Animal rights and environmental ethics are practical applications of moral principles belonging to applied ethics[cite: 211].

questions.question: How does philosophy enhance open-mindedness and tolerance?
options: By teaching that only one culture possesses absolute truth
By exposing learners to diverse, competing perspectives and revealing that intellectual achievement is an ongoing, contextual process
By forcing students to abandon all moral standards
By discouraging logical debate
questions.explanation: Studying alternative viewpoints shows the complexity of human thought, fostering tolerance, flexibility, and receptive critical thinking[cite: 214].

questions.question: Which Greek Sophist asserted the extreme skeptical claim that 'nothing exists, and that if it did, we could not know it'?
options: Socrates
Gorgias
Pythagoras
Aristotle
questions.explanation: Gorgias the Sophist expressed extreme skepticism by asserting that nothing exists, or if it does, humans cannot know it[cite: 205].

questions.question: What is the primary definition and subject matter of logic as an academic field?
options: The psychological analysis of brain function
The organized body of knowledge or science that evaluates arguments
The rhetoric of political speechmaking
The grammatical study of verb conjugations
questions.explanation: Logic is the organized body of knowledge or science that evaluates arguments and correct reasoning[cite: 219, 221, 222].

questions.question: How is an argument formally defined in logic?
options: A heated verbal disagreement or shouting match between individuals
A group of statements, one or more of which (premises) are claimed to provide support or evidence for another statement (conclusion)
A single unconditional declarative statement
A series of non-declarative questions
questions.explanation: An argument is a group of statements where the premises are claimed to provide support or reasons to believe the conclusion[cite: 224].

questions.question: What is a statement in logic, and what are its possible truth-values?
options: Any sentence whatsoever; truth-values are questions and commands
A declarative sentence that is either true or false
A proposal that is neither true nor false
An emotional exclamation
questions.explanation: A statement is a declarative sentence that has a truth-value of either true or false[cite: 224].

questions.question: Which of the following sentences qualifies as a statement in logical terms?
options: Would you please close the classroom door?
Right on!
Mekelle is the capital city of Tigray Region.
Give me your student ID card immediately!
questions.explanation: 'Mekelle is the capital city of Tigray Region' is a declarative sentence asserting a fact with a definite truth-value (true)[cite: 224, 225].

questions.question: What role does a premise play within an argument?
options: It is the main claim that the argument tries to establish
It is a statement that sets forth the reasons, evidence, or grounds for accepting the conclusion
It is a passing commentary that has no bearing on the argument
It is always a rhetorical question
questions.explanation: A premise is a statement that claims to provide evidence or reasons supporting the conclusion[cite: 225].

questions.question: Which of the following lists contains only conclusion indicator words?
options: Since, because, for the reason that, given that
Therefore, thus, consequently, accordingly, hence
Seeing that, inasmuch as, owing to, as indicated by
If, then, either, or
questions.explanation: 'Therefore', 'thus', 'consequently', 'accordingly', and 'hence' are standard conclusion indicators[cite: 227].

questions.question: Which of the following lists contains only premise indicator words?
options: Therefore, whence, wherefore, as a result
Since, because, given that, for, seeing that
It follows that, implies that, entails that
So, thus, consequently, we may conclude
questions.explanation: 'Since', 'because', 'given that', 'for', and 'seeing that' provide clues identifying premises[cite: 228].

questions.question: What is unique about the phrase 'for this reason' when identifying premises and conclusions?
options: It never appears in arguments
It occurs between the premise and conclusion: the statement before it is the premise, and the statement after it is the conclusion
It indicates that the argument is invalid
It functions exactly like 'for the reason that'
questions.explanation: 'For this reason' comes after the premise it indicates and precedes the conclusion[cite: 228].

questions.question: What two conditions must be fulfilled for a passage to purport to prove something and qualify as an argument?
options: It must use emotional language and have at least five sentences
At least one statement must claim to present evidence (factual claim), and there must be a claim that this evidence supports something (inferential claim)
It must be spoken by a licensed scientist and published in a journal
The statements must be mathematically formatted
questions.explanation: An argument requires a factual claim (alleged evidence) and an inferential claim (that the evidence implies or supports the conclusion)[cite: 231].

questions.question: How is an explicit inferential claim distinguished from an implicit inferential claim?
options: Explicit uses premise/conclusion indicator words; implicit relies on an unstated inferential relationship between statements
Explicit arguments are deductive; implicit arguments are always fallacies
Implicit arguments contain only false statements
Explicit arguments have no conclusion
questions.explanation: An explicit inferential claim is marked by indicator words ('thus', 'because'), while an implicit claim relies on structural reasoning without indicators[cite: 232].

questions.question: Why is a warning (such as 'Never confide political secrets to your wife') classified as a non-argumentative passage?
options: Because it is written in conversational prose
Because it lacks an inferential claim; no evidence is presented to prove that the statement is true
Because it contains two distinct premises
Because it uses conclusion indicators
questions.explanation: Warnings and pieces of advice state cautions or suggestions without offering evidence to establish a truth claim[cite: 234, 235].

questions.question: An expository passage is best interpreted as an argument when:
options: The topic sentence makes an obvious claim accepted by everyone
The purpose of the subsequent sentences is not merely to develop or flesh out the topic sentence, but also to prove that it is true
The passage contains no declarative statements
The sentences are arranged in alphabetical order
questions.explanation: Expository passages become arguments if the author intends the subsequent sentences to prove a controversial topic sentence[cite: 237, 238].

questions.question: What are the two structural components of an explanation?
options: Premise and conclusion
Explanandum (the phenomenon to be explained) and explanans (the statements doing the explaining)
Antecedent and consequent
Major term and minor term
questions.explanation: Every explanation consists of the explanandum (the accepted fact) and the explanans (what purports to account for it)[cite: 239].

questions.question: What is the primary logical difference between an argument and an explanation?
options: Arguments use 'because'; explanations never do
In an argument, premises aim to prove that a claim is true; in an explanation, the explanans aims to show why an already accepted fact occurred
Explanations are always valid deductive syllogisms
Arguments proceed backwards from effect to cause
questions.explanation: Arguments attempt to prove that something is the case, whereas explanations clarify why an accepted event happened[cite: 240].

questions.question: In a conditional statement ('If A, then B'), what are the component statements A and B called?
options: Premise and conclusion
Antecedent and consequent
Explanans and explanandum
Subject and predicate
questions.explanation: In an 'If... then...' statement, the component immediately following 'if' is the antecedent, and the component following 'then' is the consequent[cite: 241].

questions.question: Why is a single conditional statement NOT an argument by itself?
options: Because it contains no declarative words
Because there is no assertion that either the antecedent or consequent is actually true, and neither presents evidence to prove the other
Because conditional statements are always false
Because it has more than one conclusion
questions.explanation: A conditional statement asserts only a hypothetical relation between statements, not that either is an asserted premise proving a conclusion[cite: 242].

questions.question: How are sufficient and necessary conditions expressed in conditional statements?
options: The antecedent is a necessary condition; the consequent is a sufficient condition
The antecedent is a sufficient condition; the consequent is a necessary condition
Both antecedent and consequent are always necessary conditions
They are completely unrelated to conditional statements
questions.explanation: In 'If A, then B', the occurrence of A is sufficient for B, and B is necessary for A[cite: 244, 245].

questions.question: What defines a deductive argument?
options: An argument where the conclusion follows only with a high degree of probability
An argument incorporating the claim that it is impossible for the conclusion to be false given that the premises are true
An argument that always proceeds from specific observations to a general law
An argument whose premises are based solely on eyewitness authority
questions.explanation: A deductive argument claims that the conclusion follows necessarily and conclusively from the premises[cite: 246].

questions.question: What defines an inductive argument?
options: An argument where the premises guarantee the conclusion with 100% certainty
An argument incorporating the claim that it is improbable for the conclusion to be false given that the premises are true
An argument that cannot contain any factual claims
An argument that consists solely of a single conditional statement
questions.explanation: An inductive argument involves probabilistic reasoning: if the premises are true, the conclusion is claimed to be probably true[cite: 247].

questions.question: What three factors determine whether an argument is best interpreted as deductive or inductive?
options: The author's name, the length of the paragraph, and the date of publication
The occurrence of special indicator words, the actual strength of the inferential link, and the form of argumentation used
The number of nouns, the emotional tone, and the presence of questions
The font size, the margin width, and the inclusion of diagrams
questions.explanation: Deciding between deduction and induction depends on indicator words, the strength of the inferential link, and the argumentative form[cite: 248, 249].

questions.question: Which of the following indicator words typically signals a deductive inferential claim?
options: Plausible
Likely
Necessarily
Reasonable to conclude
questions.explanation: Words such as 'certainly', 'necessarily', 'absolutely', and 'definitely' signal deductive claims[cite: 249].

questions.question: Which of the following argumentative forms is typically classified as deductive?
options: Prediction about the weather
Argument from analogy
Argument based on mathematics (arithmetic or geometric computation)
Inductive generalization from a survey
questions.explanation: Arguments based on mathematics (excluding statistical arguments) follow necessarily and are deductive[cite: 251].

questions.question: An argument concluding that 'Angel tells the truth' because 'Angel is honest' is an example of:
options: An argument from definition (deductive)
A causal inference (inductive)
An argument from authority (inductive)
A disjunctive syllogism
questions.explanation: Arguments based on definition are deductive because the conclusion follows directly from the definition of a term[cite: 251].

questions.question: A syllogism having a conditional ('if... then...') statement for one or both of its premises is classified as:
options: A categorical syllogism
A hypothetical syllogism
A disjunctive syllogism
An inductive generalization
questions.explanation: A hypothetical syllogism is a syllogism containing conditional premises[cite: 252].

questions.question: What type of argument is: 'Rewina is either Ethiopian or Eritrean. Rewina is not Eritrean. Therefore, Rewina is Ethiopian'?
options: Inductive argument from analogy
Disjunctive syllogism (deductive)
Argument based on signs
Categorical syllogism
questions.explanation: This is a disjunctive syllogism ('either... or...'), a standard deductive argument form[cite: 252].

questions.question: An argument that proceeds from knowledge of a selected sample to a claim about an entire group is:
options: An argument from definition
An inductive generalization
A hypothetical syllogism
A mathematical proof
questions.explanation: Inductive generalizations infer attributes of an entire population based on a representative sample[cite: 253].

questions.question: Inferring that a parking space is prohibited after observing a 'No Parking' sign posted on the street is:
options: An argument based on signs (inductive)
A categorical syllogism (deductive)
An argument from analogy
A prediction
questions.explanation: Arguments based on signs infer the reality of a situation from a symbolic sign and are inductive[cite: 253, 254].

questions.question: Inferring that a water bottle left in a freezer overnight has frozen is an example of:
options: A disjunctive syllogism
A causal inference (cause to effect, inductive)
An argument from authority
A definitional deduction
questions.explanation: Reasoning from a physical cause to its expected effect is a causal inference, which is inherently probabilistic and inductive[cite: 254].

questions.question: Can deductive arguments proceed from particular premises to a general conclusion?
options: No, deduction strictly proceeds from general to particular only
Yes, deduction can proceed from particular to general (e.g., proving all odd numbers between 2 and 8 are prime)
No, only inductive arguments use particular statements
Yes, but such arguments are automatically invalid
questions.explanation: Aristotle's traditional distinction is incomplete; deductive arguments can proceed from particular to general and vice versa[cite: 254, 255].

questions.question: What is a valid deductive argument?
options: An argument that contains only true premises in the real world
An argument such that if the premises are assumed true, it is impossible for the conclusion to be false
An argument that convinces the majority of listeners
An argument with a probable conclusion
questions.explanation: Validity means the inferential connection guarantees that if premises were true, the conclusion could not be false[cite: 256].

questions.question: What is an invalid deductive argument?
options: An argument with false premises
A deductive argument such that even if the premises are assumed true, it is possible for the conclusion to be false
An argument that uses no indicator words
An argument whose conclusion is true
questions.explanation: An invalid deductive argument is one where true premises do not guarantee the conclusion; the conclusion could still be false[cite: 256].

questions.question: Which combination of truth-values in premises and conclusion automatically guarantees that a deductive argument is INVALID?
options: False premises and False conclusion
True premises and False conclusion
False premises and True conclusion
True premises and True conclusion
questions.explanation: Any deductive argument with actually true premises and an actually false conclusion is necessarily invalid[cite: 257, 258, 260].

questions.question: Can a valid deductive argument have completely false premises and a false conclusion?
options: No, valid arguments must have true premises
Yes, validity depends solely on the inferential link, not on real-world truth-values
No, that combination is logically impossible
Yes, but only if it is an inductive generalization
questions.explanation: Validity depends on the structural relationship: if premises were true, the conclusion would follow. Hence, false premises and false conclusion can form a valid argument[cite: 257, 259].

questions.question: What two conditions are required for a deductive argument to be classified as SOUND?
options: It must be inductive and strong
It must be valid and have all actually true premises
It must be clear and persuasive to a popular audience
It must have a conclusion supported by expert testimony
questions.explanation: A sound argument = a valid deductive argument + all true premises[cite: 260, 261].

questions.question: What is the truth-value of the conclusion of every sound deductive argument?
options: It is probably true
It is necessarily and strictly true
It is false
It is unknown
questions.explanation: Because a sound argument is valid and has all true premises, its conclusion is guaranteed to be true[cite: 261].

questions.question: What is an unsound deductive argument?
options: An argument that is invalid, has one or more false premises, or both
Any argument that deals with metaphysics
A strong inductive argument
An argument with a true conclusion
questions.explanation: An unsound argument is any deductive argument that is either invalid, contains at least one false premise, or both[cite: 260, 261].

questions.question: What defines a strong inductive argument?
options: An argument whose conclusion is impossible to doubt
An argument such that if the premises are assumed true, it is improbable for the conclusion to be false
An argument that has exactly two premises
An argument that uses mathematical deduction
questions.explanation: A strong inductive argument is one where true premises make the conclusion highly probable[cite: 261].

questions.question: What defines a weak inductive argument?
options: An argument whose conclusion does not follow probably from the premises, even though it is claimed to
An argument with an uneducated author
A valid deductive argument
A categorical syllogism
questions.explanation: A weak inductive argument fails its probabilistic inferential claim; even if premises are assumed true, the conclusion is not probable[cite: 261].

questions.question: How do inductive strength and weakness differ fundamentally from deductive validity and invalidity?
options: Deduction admits degrees; induction is absolute
Inductive strength admits degrees of probability and can be affected by adding new evidence; deductive validity is all-or-nothing
Inductive strength depends on grammar rules
There is no difference
questions.explanation: Unlike validity (which is absolute), inductive strength admits degrees depending on sample size and additional evidence[cite: 263].

questions.question: What two conditions make an inductive argument COGENT?
options: It must be valid and sound
It must be strong and have all actually true premises (and not overlook key evidence)
It must be popular and emotional
It must be deductive and true
questions.explanation: A cogent argument = a strong inductive argument + all true premises[cite: 265].

questions.question: What is the truth status of the conclusion of every cogent inductive argument?
options: It is guaranteed to be 100% true
It is probably true
It is necessarily false
It cannot be determined
questions.explanation: Because premises are true and the reasoning is strong, the conclusion of a cogent argument is probably true[cite: 265].

questions.question: What is an uncogent inductive argument?
options: An inductive argument that is weak, has one or more false premises, or ignores critical countervailing evidence
A valid deductive syllogism
An argument that contains a true premise
An argument with an implicit conclusion
questions.explanation: An uncogent argument is an inductive argument that is weak, contains false premises, or both[cite: 265].

questions.question: How does the true-premise requirement for cogency differ from that for soundness?
options: Cogency allows false premises
For cogency, true premises must also satisfy the total evidence requirement (not ignoring critical evidence that entails a different conclusion)
Soundness requires that premises be probable
There is no difference in the requirements
questions.explanation: Unlike soundness, cogency requires that premises do not ignore key evidence that would alter the probability of the conclusion[cite: 265].

questions.question: If an argument's premises do not support its conclusion at all, can it still be an argument?
options: No, it becomes a simple report
Yes, it is still an argument, but a bad (fallacious) argument
No, all arguments must be valid
Yes, it becomes an explanation
questions.explanation: An argument requires only the claim of support; if the premises fail to support the conclusion, it remains a bad argument[cite: 226].

questions.question: What is an 'inferential link' in logic?
options: A website hyperlink connecting articles
The reasoning connection or relationship by which premises are claimed to support the conclusion
The physical bond between sound waves in air
The punctuation mark separating paragraphs
questions.explanation: The inferential link is the logical reasoning process connecting premises to the conclusion[cite: 230].

questions.question: In evaluating an argument, which claim should always be tested first?
options: The factual claim (whether premises are true)
The inferential claim (whether premises logically support the conclusion)
The moral character of the speaker
The grammatical formatting of the sentences
questions.explanation: We test the inferential claim first; if the reasoning is flawed, the argument is worthless regardless of the truth of premises[cite: 255, 256].

questions.question: Consider: 'All African leaders are corrupt. Nelson Mandela was an African leader. Therefore, Nelson Mandela was corrupt.' This argument is:
options: Invalid and sound
Valid but unsound (because the first premise is false)
Weak and uncogent
A non-argumentative explanation
questions.explanation: The structure is deductively valid (if premises were true, conclusion would follow), but the premise is false in reality, making it unsound[cite: 256, 260, 261].

questions.question: Consider: 'This barrel contains 100 apples. 80 randomly selected apples were delicious. Therefore, probably all 100 apples are delicious.' This argument is:
options: Valid and sound
Strong inductive argument
Weak inductive argument
A deductive syllogism based on definition
questions.explanation: Sampling 80 out of 100 apples provides strong probabilistic support for the conclusion, making the argument inductively strong[cite: 261, 263].

questions.question: Why is 'Since Edison invented the phonograph, there have been many technological developments' NOT an argument?
options: Because Edison did not invent the phonograph
Because 'since' is used in a temporal sense ('from the time that') rather than a logical inferential sense
Because it contains a conclusion indicator
Because it is written in English
questions.explanation: The word 'since' here functions temporally, not as a premise indicator asserting evidence for a conclusion[cite: 233].

questions.question: What is the minimum and maximum number of conclusions an argument can have?
options: Minimum of one, maximum of infinite
Exactly one conclusion
Zero conclusions
Two conclusions
questions.explanation: By logical definition, an argument contains at least one premise, but one and only one conclusion[cite: 225].

questions.question: What is philosophy of language?
options: The study of Latin verb conjugations
The reasoned inquiry into the origins of language, nature of meaning, usage, cognition, and relation between language and reality
The mechanical typesetting of dictionaries
The clinical treatment of speech disorders
questions.explanation: Philosophy of language investigates meaning, language usage, cognition, and the relationship between language and reality[cite: 271].

questions.question: How did linguist Noam Chomsky characterize human language acquisition?
options: Language is learned purely by behavioral trial and error
Humans are born with an innate understanding of 'universal grammar', and exposure triggers this knowledge
Language is solely determined by written scripts
There are no shared linguistic principles among humans
questions.explanation: Chomsky argues that humans possess an innate 'universal grammar' that structures language acquisition[cite: 272].

questions.question: What is the view of Semantic Holism regarding linguistic meaning?
options: Every word has a single dictionary definition
Meaning cannot be associated with an isolated word or sentence, but only attributed to an entire language
Meaning is completely determined by facial gestures
Words have no real reference to the world
questions.explanation: Semantic Holism holds that meaning belongs to a whole language system rather than isolated individual words[cite: 272].

questions.question: Which philosophical theory of meaning, associated with Ludwig Wittgenstein, understands meaning as related to speech acts and practical utterances?
options: Idea theory
Use theory
Truth-conditional theory
Verificationist theory
questions.explanation: Wittgenstein's Use theory identifies meaning with the practical application and social use of words in speech acts[cite: 274].

questions.question: The Verificationist theory of meaning, adopted by 20th-century Logical Positivists, asserts that:
options: Words have meaning only if sanctified by religious authorities
The meaning of a sentence is equivalent to its method of empirical verification or falsification
All words are innate mental symbols
Meaning is determined by emotional feelings
questions.explanation: Verificationism equates the cognitive meaning of a statement with its method of empirical verification[cite: 274].

questions.question: What two linguistic functions are of paramount importance for the study of logic?
options: Telling jokes and singing songs
Conveying information (cognitive meaning) and expressing or evoking feelings (emotive meaning)
Asking questions and issuing legal commands
Greeting people and flirting
questions.explanation: Logic focuses on language that conveys information (cognitive) versus language that expresses or evokes feelings (emotive)[cite: 276].

questions.question: Why must logicians disengage the cognitive meaning of emotively charged statements from their emotive meaning?
options: Because logic is concerned with evaluating arguments based on factual and inferential claims rather than emotional manipulation
Because words with emotive meaning have no definitions
Because emotions are grammatically illegal in sentences
Because logic cannot analyze declarative sentences
questions.explanation: Logic evaluates truth claims and reasoning; emotive language obscures value claims and creates psychological bias[cite: 277].

questions.question: What is a 'value claim' in the cognitive content of an emotive statement?
options: A monetary estimate of market price
A claim that something is good, bad, right, wrong, better, or worse, which requires supporting evidence
A mathematical calculation of volume
A non-syntactic arrangement of terms
questions.explanation: A value claim asserts that something is morally or qualitatively good/bad/right/wrong, demanding logical justification[cite: 277].

questions.question: How does emotive terminology function like a 'steamroller' in poor arguments?
options: It crushes physical obstacles on roads
It exerts psychological pressure that tends to paralyze critical thought and obscure the absence of evidence for value claims
It turns deductive arguments into sound deductions
It provides rigorous scientific data
questions.explanation: Emotive language intimidates or seduces listeners, suppressing critical scrutiny of unevidenced value claims[cite: 277, 278].

questions.question: When is a linguistic expression classified as VAGUE?
options: When it has two distinct, crystal-clear meanings
When there are borderline cases where it is impossible to tell if the expression applies or does not apply (meaning is hazy and blurred)
When it contains mathematical equations
When it is translated from Latin
questions.explanation: Vagueness involves hazy borders where meaning allows a continuous range of uncertain interpretations (e.g., 'fresh', 'rich')[cite: 279].

questions.question: When is a linguistic expression classified as AMBIGUOUS?
options: When it can be interpreted as having more than one clearly distinct meaning in a given context
When its letters are misspelled
When it lacks emotional vocabulary
When it refers to an empty class
questions.explanation: Ambiguity arises when a word or phrase can mean multiple discrete, distinct things in a context (e.g., 'bank', 'light')[cite: 280].

questions.question: How do verbal disputes differ from factual disputes in logic?
options: Verbal disputes center on disagreements over the meanings of words; factual disputes center on disagreements over the facts themselves
Verbal disputes occur in writing; factual disputes are spoken
Verbal disputes are always sound arguments
There is no distinction between them
questions.explanation: Verbal disputes arise from linguistic ambiguity or vagueness; factual disputes concern objective truth/falsity of factual claims[cite: 281, 282].

questions.question: What is a TERM in logic?
options: Any single word in a dictionary
Any word or arrangement of words that may serve as the subject of a statement (proper names, common names, descriptive phrases)
Any punctuation mark in a sentence
An exclamation or question
questions.explanation: A term is any word or group of words that can serve as the subject of a proposition[cite: 282].

questions.question: Which of the following expressions is NOT a term according to logical definitions?
options: The Ethiopian Parliament
Those who study hard
Runs quickly into the forest
Abebe
questions.explanation: 'Runs quickly into the forest' consists of verbs, adverbs, and prepositions that cannot serve as the subject of a statement[cite: 283].

questions.question: What is the difference between using a word and mentioning a word?
options: Using a word applies it to an object; mentioning a word treats the word itself as the object of discourse (usually in quotes)
Mentioning a word makes it an argument
Using a word is always informal
There is no difference
questions.explanation: A word is used to speak about things, but mentioned when the word itself is spoken about (e.g., 'Wherever' is an eight-letter word)[cite: 283].

questions.question: What is the INTENSIONAL meaning (connotation) of a term?
options: The individual physical members of the class denoted by the term
The qualities, attributes, or characteristics that the term connotes
The monetary market value of the object
The grammatical suffix of the word
questions.explanation: Intensional meaning (connotation or sense) consists of the properties or attributes a term connotes[cite: 283].

questions.question: What is the EXTENSIONAL meaning (denotation) of a term?
options: The abstract qualities of the term
The members of the class that the term denotes
The emotional mood evoked by the term
The dictionary pronunciation of the term
questions.explanation: Extensional meaning (denotation or reference) consists of the actual entities belonging to the class the term denotes[cite: 283].

questions.question: What is 'conventional connotation' in logic?
options: A person's idiosyncratic subjective emotions toward a word
The attributes that the term commonly calls forth in the minds of competent speakers of the language
The legal trademark registration of a word
The grammatical syntax of poetry
questions.explanation: Conventional connotation avoids private subjective biases by focusing on shared attributes recognized by competent speakers[cite: 283, 284].

questions.question: What does it mean for a term to have EMPTY EXTENSION?
options: It has no intension and no meaning
It denotes the empty (null) class having no living or existing members (e.g., 'currently living dodo bird', 'unicorn')
It cannot be pronounced
It is an invalid argument
questions.explanation: A term has empty extension when no physical members currently exist in the class it denotes, even though its intension is meaningful[cite: 284].

questions.question: What is the fundamental rule governing the relationship between intension and extension?
options: Extension determines intension
Intension determines extension
Intension and extension are always mutually exclusive
They vary randomly with the weather
questions.explanation: Intension determines extension: the connoted attributes establish the criteria for determining class membership[cite: 284, 285].

questions.question: Which of the following series of terms is arranged in the order of INCREASING INTENSION?
options: Tiger, feline, mammal, animal
Animal, mammal, feline, tiger
Animal, tiger, mammal, feline
Feline, tiger, animal, mammal
questions.explanation: Increasing intension moves from the most general to the most specific, adding attributes: animal -> mammal -> feline -> tiger[cite: 285].

questions.question: Which of the following series of terms is arranged in the order of INCREASING EXTENSION?
options: Animal, mammal, feline, tiger
Tiger, feline, mammal, animal
Tiger, animal, feline, mammal
Mammal, animal, tiger, feline
questions.explanation: Increasing extension moves from smaller class sizes to larger class sizes: tiger -> feline -> mammal -> animal[cite: 285].

questions.question: In logic, what are the two essential parts of every definition?
options: Premise and conclusion
Definiendum (word to be defined) and definiens (group of words doing the defining)
Antecedent and consequent
Subject and predicate
questions.explanation: Every definition consists of the definiendum (what is defined) and the definiens (what does the defining)[cite: 287].

questions.question: What is a STIPULATIVE definition?
options: A definition that reports the conventional dictionary meaning
A definition that assigns a meaning to a word for the first time (coining a new word or giving a new meaning to an old word)
A definition that reduces vagueness in legal courts
A definition that evokes negative emotions
questions.explanation: A stipulative definition introduces a meaning to a symbol or word for the first time[cite: 288].

questions.question: Can a stipulative definition be evaluated as strictly true or false?
options: Yes, if it contradicts dictionary entries
No, because it is an arbitrary assignment of meaning, not an assertion of fact
Yes, if verified by an empirical experiment
Only if it is a mathematical equation
questions.explanation: Because stipulative definitions assign meaning arbitrarily for the first time, they have no truth-value (cannot be true or false)[cite: 288, 289].

questions.question: What is the primary purpose of a LEXICAL definition?
options: To invent secret military codes
To report the meaning that a word already has in common usage and eliminate ambiguity
To establish speculative scientific theories
To manipulate public political attitudes
questions.explanation: Lexical definitions report established usage in a language (like a dictionary) and prevent ambiguity[cite: 289].

questions.question: What is the primary function of a PRÉCISING definition?
options: To evoke strong feelings of anger
To reduce the vagueness of a word so a decision can be reached in specific legal, medical, or technical contexts
To create fictional creatures
To replace an entire language
questions.explanation: Précising definitions reduce vagueness, clarifying borderline cases for specialized contexts like law or medicine[cite: 290].

questions.question: Defining 'moment of death' as the cessation of brain activity as measured by an electroencephalograph is an example of:
options: A persuasive definition
A précising definition
A stipulative definition
An etymological definition
questions.explanation: This establishes a precise boundary for medical and legal determinations, functioning as a précising definition[cite: 290, 291].

questions.question: What is a THEORETICAL definition?
options: A definition assigning meaning by proposing a theory that characterizes the entity and suggests experimental consequences
A definition consisting of a single synonym
An emotional speech delivered in parliament
A demonstration pointing at a physical object
questions.explanation: Theoretical definitions explain concepts (e.g., heat as molecular kinetic energy) in the context of an overarching theory[cite: 291].

questions.question: A definition intended to engender a favorable or unfavorable emotional attitude toward the definiendum (e.g., 'Abortion means the ruthless murdering of innocent babies') is:
options: A lexical definition
A persuasive definition
An operational definition
A demonstrative definition
questions.explanation: Persuasive definitions use value-laden, emotive terms to influence attitudes toward the definiendum[cite: 292].

questions.question: What is an extensional (denotative) definitional technique?
options: Assigning meaning by indicating the individual members or subclasses of the class denoted by the term
Providing a single grammatical synonym
Tracing the Greek and Latin roots of a word
Specifying an experimental laboratory operation
questions.explanation: Extensional techniques identify meaning by pointing to or naming the members of the class[cite: 293].

questions.question: A definition in which the definiens consists at least partly of a physical gesture of pointing at an object is:
options: An enumerative definition
A demonstrative (ostensive) definition
An etymological definition
A synonymous definition
questions.explanation: Demonstrative or ostensive definitions define terms by physically pointing to instances of the object[cite: 293].

questions.question: Defining 'Actor' as 'a person such as Abebe Balicha, Samsom Taddesse, or Mahder Assefa' is an example of:
options: An operational definition
An enumerative definition
A definition by genus and difference
An etymological definition
questions.explanation: Enumerative definitions assign meaning by naming individual members of the class denoted by the term[cite: 294].

questions.question: Defining 'Tree' as 'an oak, pine, elm, spruce, or maple' is:
options: A demonstrative definition
A definition by subclass
A theoretical definition
A synonymous definition
questions.explanation: Definition by subclass identifies the meaning of a general term by naming specific subclasses within it[cite: 294, 295].

questions.question: Why do all extensional definitions suffer from inherent deficiencies?
options: Because extension determines intension
Because listing members cannot definitively communicate the intended intensional attributes (extensions suggest intensions, but cannot determine them)
Because no words can be defined extensionally
Because physical objects cannot be pointed at
questions.explanation: Extensional definitions cannot guarantee that the listener understands the precise attributes meant by the term[cite: 295, 296].

questions.question: What is a SYNONYMOUS definition?
options: A definition where the definiens is a single word connoting the same attributes as the definiendum
A definition requiring a chemistry laboratory
A definition that traces linguistic root ancestry
A definition dividing a class into five subclasses
questions.explanation: A synonymous definition equates the term with another single word sharing the same meaning (e.g., 'Physician' means doctor)[cite: 296].

questions.question: An ETYMOLOGICAL definition assigns meaning by:
options: Measuring brain waves
Disclosing the word's linguistic ancestry and root origins
Naming the members of a set
Pointing an index finger at a specimen
questions.explanation: Etymological definitions trace a word's ancestral roots in its native or parent languages[cite: 297].

questions.question: Which type of definition specifies experimental procedures that determine whether the term applies to a given phenomenon?
options: Synonymous definition
Operational definition
Persuasive definition
Ostensive definition
questions.explanation: Operational definitions define concepts through specific physical procedures or tests (e.g., litmus paper turning red)[cite: 297, 298].

questions.question: In logic, what does 'definition by genus and difference' combine to define a species term?
options: An emotional adjective and a verb
A relatively larger class term (genus) and the distinguishing attribute(s) (specific difference)
Two synonymous words
A proper name and a date
questions.explanation: It identifies a broader category (genus) and the specific attribute that sets the subclass apart (difference)[cite: 298, 299].

questions.question: In the definition ''Ice' means frozen water', what are the species, specific difference, and genus respectively?
options: Species = frozen; difference = water; genus = ice
Species = ice; difference = frozen; genus = water
Species = water; difference = ice; genus = frozen
Species = ice; difference = water; genus = temperature
questions.explanation: Ice is the species term, water is the broader genus, and frozen is the specific difference[cite: 299].

questions.question: Why is 'A bird is any warm-blooded animal having wings' defective as a lexical definition?
options: It is grammatically incorrect
It is too broad, because it mistakenly includes bats (which are mammals, not birds)
It is too narrow, because it excludes robins
It is intrinsically circular
questions.explanation: The definition is too broad: the definiens applies to bats, which are warm-blooded and have wings[cite: 301].

questions.question: Why is 'A bird is any warm-blooded, feathered animal that can fly' defective as a lexical definition?
options: It is too broad
It is too narrow, because it excludes flightless birds such as ostriches and penguins
It contains affective language
It is an operational definition
questions.explanation: The definition is too narrow: it fails to include birds that cannot fly, such as ostriches[cite: 301, 302].

questions.question: The pair of definitions ''Science' means the activity engaged in by scientists' and ''Scientist' means anyone who engages in science' violates which rule of lexical definition?
options: Avoid obscure language
Avoid circularity
Be affirmative rather than negative
Indicate the context
questions.explanation: These definitions are circular: each term is defined entirely in terms of the other[cite: 302].

questions.question: Defining 'Concord' as 'the absence of discord' violates which lexical rule when an affirmative definition ('harmony') is available?
options: Conform to proper grammar
Avoid circularity
A lexical definition should not be negative when it can be affirmative
Avoid technical language
questions.explanation: Definitions should be affirmative whenever possible, rather than defining something merely by what it lacks[cite: 302].

questions.question: Defining 'Camel' as 'a ship of the desert' violates which rule of lexical definition?
options: Avoid circularity
Avoid figurative or metaphorical language
Avoid narrowness
Indicate the context
questions.explanation: Metaphorical or figurative descriptions paint pictures rather than conveying literal essential meanings[cite: 303].

questions.question: Defining 'Bunny' as 'a mammalian of the family Leporidae of the order Lagomorpha' violates the rule against:
options: Negative definitions
Obscure and needlessly technical language
Circularity
Grammatical incorrectness
questions.explanation: Overly technical, obscure language should be avoided for common, non-technical words[cite: 303].

questions.question: A definition stating ''Communism' means that brilliant invention of Karl Marx and other foolish visionaries...' violates the rule against:
options: Avoid affective and emotionally sarcastic terminology
Conform to grammar
Avoid broad definitions
Indicate the context
questions.explanation: Affective terminology plays on emotions through sarcasm and biases rather than giving objective meaning[cite: 304].

questions.question: Why do definitions of words like 'Strike' require explicit reference to the context to which the definiens pertains?
options: Because 'Strike' has empty extension
Because 'Strike' has distinctly different meanings in baseball, bowling, and industrial labor
Because 'Strike' is an invalid syllogism
Because 'Strike' has no intensional meaning
questions.explanation: Rule 8 specifies that words with different contextual meanings must indicate their specialized domain[cite: 304].

questions.question: Can proper names serve as terms according to the rules of logic?
options: No, only common nouns can be terms
Yes, proper names can serve as the subject of a statement and denote individuals
Only if they are written in Greek
Only when used as adverbs
questions.explanation: Proper names (e.g., 'Abebe', 'The Ethiopian Parliament') are terms because they serve as subjects of propositions[cite: 282, 284].

questions.question: When pure silicon turns into an acid in a chemistry problem, defining an acid as 'having a pH of less than 7' fails to be an operational definition because:
options: It is completely false
It prescribes no specific physical or experimental operation to be performed
It is an enumerative definition
It is too narrow
questions.explanation: An operational definition must specify an action or test (such as immersing litmus paper); stating a value alone is not an operation[cite: 297, 298].

questions.question: How is critical thinking fundamentally defined in the module?
options: The passive memorization and recitation of facts on examinations
A wide range of cognitive skills and intellectual dispositions needed to effectively identify, analyze, and evaluate arguments and truth claims
The habit of aggressively criticizing other people's personal character
The unquestioning acceptance of established traditions
questions.explanation: Critical thinking encompasses cognitive skills and intellectual dispositions to evaluate claims and overcome biases[cite: 310].

questions.question: How did American philosopher John Dewey define critical thinking?
options: The memorization of encyclopedic knowledge
Active, persistent, and careful consideration of a belief or supposed knowledge in light of the grounds supporting it and further conclusions to which it tends
Unreflective, impulsive reaction to daily life events
Thinking that seeks to maximize personal financial profit
questions.explanation: Dewey defined critical thinking as an active, persistent, and careful examination of beliefs and their supporting grounds[cite: 311].

questions.question: Why did John Dewey characterize critical thinking as an 'active' process?
options: It involves physical jogging while studying
The thinker raises questions, gathers evidence, and thinks things through for oneself rather than passively receiving information from others
It makes rapid decisions without reflection
It rejects all forms of reading
questions.explanation: For Dewey, active thinking means questioning and reasoning independently rather than passively absorbing external claims[cite: 311].

questions.question: How did Robert Ennis define critical thinking in his influential contribution to the field?
options: Mechanical deduction based on symbolic tables
Reasonable, reflective thinking focused on deciding what to believe or do
The automatic acceptance of authoritative dogmas
Thinking that avoids all forms of practical decision-making
questions.explanation: Robert Ennis defined critical thinking as reasonable, reflective thinking focused on deciding what to believe or do[cite: 312].

questions.question: What is 'meta-cognition' in Richard Paul's conception of critical thinking?
options: Thinking about one's own thinking, with the aim of consciously improving its quality against intellectual standards
Memorizing neurological anatomy
A form of mystical extrasensory perception
Subconscious wishful thinking
questions.explanation: Meta-cognition is 'thinking about one's thinking', consciously monitoring and improving its rationality[cite: 312].

questions.question: Why do some theorists use the term 'criticocreative' thinking instead of simply critical thinking?
options: Because critical thinking requires artistic painting
To emphasize that good critical evaluation is not just negative fault-finding, but requires creative imagination to formulate alternative hypotheses and perspectives
To indicate that critical thinking is entirely emotional
Because critical thinking avoids logical rules
questions.explanation: 'Criticocreative' highlights that evaluating ideas requires creativity to envision alternative scenarios, points of view, and solutions[cite: 313, 314].

questions.question: Which critical thinking standard is considered the 'gateway standard', without which one cannot evaluate accuracy or relevance?
options: Consistency
Clarity
Completeness
Fairness
questions.explanation: Clarity is the gateway standard: if an assertion is unclear or vague, one cannot determine whether it is true, accurate, or relevant[cite: 315].

questions.question: The standard of PRECISION in critical thinking involves:
options: Speaking in broad, hazy generalities
Insisting on exact, detailed, and careful answers to specific questions
Using emotional appeals to convince audiences
Rejecting all mathematical models
questions.explanation: Precision requires cutting through ambiguities by demanding specific, exact details and careful distinctions[cite: 316].

questions.question: How does John Rawls describe the primary importance of truth (accuracy) in 'A Theory of Justice'?
options: Truth is secondary to political consensus
Truth is the first virtue of systems of thought; an elegant theory must be rejected or revised if it is untrue
Truth is entirely a subjective matter of opinion
Truth depends on the speaker's status
questions.explanation: Rawls emphasized that no matter how elegant a theory is, it must be rejected if it lacks truth and accuracy[cite: 316].

questions.question: The critical thinking standard of RELEVANCE focuses on:
options: Raising sensational topics to distract listeners
Ensuring that statements have a genuine logical connection and bearing on the specific issue at hand
Gathering massive quantities of unrelated trivia
Verifying the monetary value of evidence
questions.explanation: Relevance demands that ideas and evidence bear directly upon the truth or merit of the claim being evaluated[cite: 317].

questions.question: What is the difference between logical inconsistency and practical inconsistency?
options: Logical involves saying or believing contradictory things; practical involves saying one thing and doing another (hypocrisy)
Logical applies to science; practical applies to grammar
Practical is always conscious; logical is always accidental
There is no difference
questions.explanation: Logical inconsistency is holding contradictory beliefs; practical inconsistency is a contradiction between one's professed beliefs and actual actions[cite: 317].

questions.question: The standard of FAIRNESS in critical thinking demands that our thinking be:
options: Biased exclusively toward our family and ethnic group
Open-minded, impartial, and free of distorting self-interest or preconceptions
Hostile to unfamiliar ideas
Governed entirely by peer pressure
questions.explanation: Fairness requires treating all relevant viewpoints impartially without privileging self-serving biases[cite: 319].

questions.question: According to the STRUCTURAL PRINCIPLE of a good argument:
options: An argument must contain at least five paragraphs
An argument must be structurally well-formed, using premises that do not contradict each other or the conclusion, and drawing no invalid inferences
An argument must be phrased in Latin
An argument must use rhetorical questions
questions.explanation: The structural principle requires that premises are mutually compatible and lead legitimately to the conclusion without contradiction[cite: 320, 321].

questions.question: The RELEVANCE PRINCIPLE of a good argument requires an arguer to:
options: Provide reasons whose truth provides actual evidence or counts in favor of the conclusion
Use only arguments from famous authorities
Appeal to the audience's deep emotional pity
Avoid deductive syllogisms
questions.explanation: The relevance principle states that an arguer must present only reasons that bear directly upon the truth of the conclusion[cite: 321].

questions.question: Why is the term 'acceptable' preferred over the traditional term 'true' in the ACCEPTABILITY PRINCIPLE of good arguments?
options: Because truth does not exist
Because absolute truth is notoriously difficult to establish conclusively in informal discussions, making 'accepted as true by a rational person' more practical
Because acceptability allows an arguer to use obvious lies
Because logic rejects factual claims
questions.explanation: Acceptability is practical: it requires reasons that a mature, rational person would accept in light of available evidence[cite: 322].

questions.question: The SUFFICIENCY PRINCIPLE of a good argument requires that:
options: An arguer present at least ten separate premises
The premises provided are sufficient in number, kind, and weight to justify acceptance of the conclusion
The premises be identical to the conclusion
The argument omit all counter-evidence
questions.explanation: The sufficiency principle requires that relevant and acceptable reasons carry enough collective weight to justify the conclusion[cite: 323].

questions.question: The REBUTTAL PRINCIPLE requires a good argument to:
options: Attack the opponent's moral character directly
Anticipate and effectively respond to serious criticisms and counterarguments brought against the position
Ignore all objections raised by critics
Change the topic of discussion to something flashy
questions.explanation: A complete, good argument must anticipate and effectively refute serious counterarguments[cite: 323, 324].

questions.question: The FALLIBILITY PRINCIPLE in critical thinking requires each participant to:
options: Insist that their own personal beliefs are 100% infallible
Acknowledge that one's own initial position may be wrong or not the most defensible view on the issue
Refuse to listen to opponents
Accept every argument presented without scrutiny
questions.explanation: The fallibility principle requires an honest admission that one might be mistaken, which is essential for rational discussion[cite: 325].

questions.question: What does the BURDEN OF PROOF PRINCIPLE require in a rational discussion?
options: The listener must always disprove any claim made by the speaker
The burden of proof rests on the participant who sets forth a position, who is obligated to produce reasons if challenged
No one is ever required to give evidence
The oldest person in the room carries the burden of proof
questions.explanation: Anyone making a positive or negative claim has the logical obligation to provide supporting reasons when asked[cite: 326, 327].

questions.question: What does the PRINCIPLE OF CHARITY require when reformulating an opponent's argument?
options: Distorting the argument into a ridiculous caricature to defeat it easily
Expressing the opponent's argument in its strongest possible version consistent with their original intention
Donating money to the opponent before arguing
Ignoring all the opponent's premises
questions.explanation: Charity requires evaluating the best, strongest interpretation of an opponent's argument[cite: 327].

questions.question: The SUSPENSION OF JUDGMENT PRINCIPLE states that:
options: One should always make a snap judgment immediately
If no position is defended by a good argument, or competing positions are defended with equal strength, one should suspend judgment
One should flip a coin to decide complex ethical issues
Judges in courtrooms should never issue verdicts
questions.explanation: When evidence is insufficient or evenly balanced on both sides, suspending judgment is the rational response[cite: 327, 328].

questions.question: The RESOLUTION PRINCIPLE states that an issue should be considered settled when:
options: The loudest arguer silences the room
An argument for one position is structurally sound, uses relevant and acceptable reasons sufficient to justify the conclusion, and provides effective rebuttals
The government bans all further discussion of the topic
Both sides agree to disagree permanently
questions.explanation: An issue is resolved when an argument fulfills all criteria of a good argument and out-reasons competing alternatives[cite: 328].

questions.question: Which of the following is a basic intellectual trait of a CRITICAL thinker?
options: Pretending to know more than one actually does
Being honest with oneself, acknowledging limitations, and being watchful of personal errors
Regarding controversial issues as annoying threats to one's ego
Basing decisions entirely on first impressions and gut reactions
questions.explanation: Critical thinkers practice intellectual honesty, recognizing their ignorance and revising judgments in the face of evidence[cite: 330, 331].

questions.question: Which of the following is a characteristic trait of an UNCRITICAL thinker?
options: Remaining patient with complexity and investing time to understand issues
Being impatient with complexity and preferring confusion over the effort to understand
Striving to see both sides of an issue
Thinking before acting
questions.explanation: Uncritical thinkers are impatient with complex nuance, clinging stubbornly to initial impressions[cite: 331].

questions.question: What is EGOCENTRISM as a major barrier to critical thinking?
options: The tendency to view reality as centered entirely on oneself, viewing one's own interests and values as superior to others
